classes.fixPattern: Stop assuming verse (and, where relevant, chapter) coordinates from own-versification stores are dense integers. The canonical fix WIN should apply at every site: treat verse keys as opaque ordered labels. (1) For web_content.api_compare (lines ~104-136): drop the `max_verse = max(...)` + `range(1, max_verse+1)` dense-integer reconstruction entirely; instead build the union of actual verse keys across translations and emit rows in a versification-aware order — e.g. `all_verse_keys = sorted(set().union(*(by_t[t].keys() for t in known)), key=_verse_sort_key)` where `_verse_sort_key` parses a leading integer + optional letter suffix (so 1,2,'2a',3 sort correctly and pure-int stores are byte-identical), then iterate those keys (not range), and set verse_count = len(all_verse_keys). Never call max()/range()/+1 on a verse value. (2) For any `int(verse)`/`int(chapter)` coercion of store- or note-derived coords (verse_of_day:200), guard with a label-aware parse: keep the value as-is when it is not a pure integer (split numeric prefix from letter suffix into the existing `suffix` field rather than int()-crashing), or skip own-vers coords for features that require integer ordering. (3) For int-keyed verse dicts (preview notes_by_verse): key on the verse value's canonical string form (str(v)) on BOTH the build and lookup side so int and str labels match, instead of assuming an int key. General rule: a (ch,v) value that can originate from get_chapter()/get_verse()/_load_book() of a VERSIFICATION=='own' store, or from a note that mirrors such a store, must flow through a single shared label-safe comparator/sorter (add a helper e.g. translations.verse_sort_key) — never raw int()/max()/min()/range()/'+1'/'<'/sum() arithmetic. Add a test that feeds api_compare and preview a synthetic own-vers book containing a lettered verse label ('B1') and asserts no TypeError/ValueError and correct ordering, to keep the whole class closed.

sites.why: all_verse_nums is built from by_t[t].keys() where by_t[t] = {row[0]: row[1] for row in get_chapter(t, book, chapter_n)}. api_compare accepts ANY id in list_translations(), which includes the own-versification stores geez-tewahedo / geez-tewahedo-en (VERSIFICATION=='own'). For an own-vers book, get_chapter's row[0] can be a STRING verse label (the po_vision_store contract explicitly allows e.g. 'B1' Esther/LXX-Addition labels). max() over a set mixing/containing str raises TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'. This is the originally-reported sibling of translations.get_chapter and the strongest live in-class site.

Same data flow: max_verse is the max over own-vers-capable verse keys. range(1, max_verse + 1) requires max_verse to be an int; a string label makes both `max_verse + 1` and range() raise TypeError. Even if max() somehow returned a str, this line cannot consume it. Part of the same api_compare defect; the per-verse alignment loop assumes a dense 1..N integer verse space that own-versification (lettered/sparse labels) does not provide.

int(spec.chapter)/int(spec.verse) coerce NoteSpec coords read from content/notes/<book>.py. The note-tuple schema documents verse as int with a separate suffix field, and no on-disk note currently carries a str verse (verified: 0 non-int (ch,vs) across content/notes). But this is the same int-assuming pattern: if an own-vers / Addition-labelled note verse ('B1') ever lands in the corpus, int('B1') raises ValueError. Reported as a confirmed consumer; today latent (defensive coercion would crash rather than degrade).

preview.api_preview_chapter calls translations.get_chapter(translation_id, ...) for an arbitrary translation_id (not hard-coded kjv), then keys notes_by_verse on the int note verse and looks it up with vnum from get_chapter rows. classes.className: Unauthenticated public emitters interpolating corpus-derived strings into HTML/XML without uniformly-applied, CDATA-safe escaping (RSS feed / live server-rendered markup routes)
classes.fixPattern: Make CDATA-safety a single enforced chokepoint instead of a per-field emergent property. Introduce one helper, e.g. `def _cdata(s: str) -> str: return _xml_escape(...)`-free raw HTML wrapped as `\"<![CDATA[\" + str(s).replace(\"]]>\", \"]]]]><![CDATA[>\") + \"]]>\"` (the standard split-the-terminator idiom), and route the ENTIRE `description` string (ref + label + body) through it exactly once at emit time — so every present and future field interpolated into the CDATA section is neutralized by construction, not by remembering to `_xml_escape` each one. Then drop the ad-hoc `.replace(\"]]>\", \"]]>\")` on `safe_body` (now redundant). For the non-CDATA fields, keep `_xml_escape` but assert it is applied at the single emit point. Canonical rule WIN should apply at every public-emitter site: corpus strings entering an XML/HTML emitter must pass through exactly one context-appropriate escaper chosen by the emit context (element-text/attr → `_xml_escape`; CDATA → `_cdata`; HTML body → `sanitize_html`), with no field interpolated raw and no per-field exceptions.

sites.why: CANONICAL SITE of the class. This `description` string is interpolated whole into `<![CDATA[{description}]]>` (line 353) on the unauthenticated public route /api/verse-of-day.rss, which walks the entire notes corpus. CDATA-breakout safety is achieved by TWO different mechanisms applied to different fields: (a) `safe_body` gets an explicit `.replace("]]>", "]]>")`, while (b) `ref` and `label` are only `_xml_escape`'d. It currently holds (because `_xml_escape` escapes `>`, so a `]]>` in ref/label incidentally becomes `]]>`), but the CDATA-safety of this block is NOT enforced by a single chokepoint — it is an emergent property of two separate escapers. Any future field added to `description` without one of those two treatments silently breaks out of the CDATA section and injects raw XML. This is exactly the 'CDATA-escape depending on sanitize_html ordering / _xml_escape coverage must be complete on EVERY interpolated field' risk named in the class.

CDATA contexts are NOT made safe by `_xml_escape` semantics alone — they require `]]>` neutralization. classes.className: Shared process-global _CACHED_CONN (sqlite3.connect(check_same_thread=False)) is READ — conn.execute() — outside _CONN_LOCK by every query helper, while invalidate()/rebuild()/_build_to() can close that same handle under the lock; the lock makes the close/swap atomic but does NOT span the reader's execute, so each reader/writer pair is a use-after-close race window under ThreadingHTTPServer + the build ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=5).
classes.fixPattern:
Make _CONN_LOCK span the actual query, not just the open/close, so a reader and a closer can never overlap on the same handle. The canonical fix WIN should apply at EVERY reader site: replace the `conn = connection(); ... conn.execute(...)` pattern with a single context-managed helper that holds _CONN_LOCK for the whole read. Concretely, add to corpus_index.py:

    @contextlib.contextmanager
    def _read_cursor():
        with _CONN_LOCK:
            conn = _ensure_conn()   # the body of connection() AFTER rebuild(), i.e. the open/swap, run while already holding the lock; rebuild() itself stays OUTSIDE the lock as today
            yield conn              # invalidate()/rebuild()/_build_to() also take _CONN_LOCK to close, so they now block until the reader's execute+fetchall completes

and rewrite every helper (count_by_kind, count_by_book, count_by_kind_and_book, total_note_count, kinds_present, audit_attribution, compute_matrix_indexed, search, fts5_search, dashboard_stats) as `with _read_cursor() as conn: rows = conn.execute(...).fetchall()` — crucially fetching ALL rows inside the `with` so no lazy cursor escapes the lock. Because sqlite serialises in default threadsafety mode this is correct and the lock is held only for the (sub-ms, indexed) query. WorkCache (scripts/core/work_cache.py) already demonstrates this exact pattern (every get/put runs its execute inside self._lock) and is the reference implementation. Alternative if per-query locking is too coarse for audit_attribution/dashboard's full scans: switch each reader to open its OWN short-lived sqlite3.connect(_index_path()) (read-only, mode=ro) and close it in a finally — then there is no shared handle to close out from under anyone and _CACHED_CONN can be retired entirely. Either way the invariant is: no thread may call conn.execute on _CACHED_CONN while another thread can close it; today the lock guards only the close, leaving every execute exposed.

classes.className: Migration runner ok:False handling + each migration's idempotency / version-awareness / down() / first-run consistency — the runner treats any ok:False as a hard stop that aborts the whole chain, while migration 0002 is designed to RETURN ok:False as a routine "soft failure" once a tradition-tagged corpus lands; 0001 + the launcher's first-run copy use a non-version-aware force=False shutil copy that the ledger runner never gates; and the wrapped main()s are called with mismatched argv contracts.
classes.fixPattern: Make the runner's result contract tri-state instead of binary, and route every wrapped/first-run copy through it version-aware. Concretely WIN should: (1) In scripts/migrate.py, give a migration's up() a third outcome beyond ok:True/ok:False — e.g. a `skipped`/`blocked`/`deferred` flag (or `ok:True, applied:False, reason:...`). run_up must treat an intentional 'not-yet-applicable' result as a non-fatal SKIP (do NOT record in the ledger, do NOT abort the chain, continue to later migrations, exit 0 with a warning) and reserve abort+exit-1 strictly for genuine hard failures (exceptions / corrupt state). (2) Convert 0002's `ok:False`-on-pending-rewrites to that new soft/deferred outcome so a future tradition-tagged corpus warns-and-continues rather than wedging every launch. (3) Fix the argv contract: give backfill_traditions.main(argv=None) an argv parameter and call p.parse_args(argv); have 0001/0002 pass main([]) (and migrate_to_user_data.main([]) already does) so the wrapped scripts never inherit the runner's sys.argv. (4) Make the copy version-aware: stamp a schema/content version (e.g. a VERSION file or editions.yaml `content_version`) and have perform_migration overwrite when the bundled version is newer (mtime/hash or version compare) rather than force=False blanket-skip; route the launcher's bootstrap_user_data through the same ledger/runner so first-run + 0001 share one version state instead of two independent force=False copies. (5) Keep down() raising NotImplementedError but ensure the runner surfaces forward_only as a clear non-crash (already done for migrate.py; mirror the same explicit tri-state in core/migrate.py and make the DDL+bookkeeping INSERT atomic in one transaction so the DB can never get ahead of the ledger).

It only distinguishes 'never migrated' vs 'migrated'; it cannot detect a partial/aborted copy or a newer bundled schema, so a half-copied user-data dir is treated as fully migrated and never repaired. Version-awareness/first-run gap of the copy class.

sites.snippet: with conn: conn.executescript(sql); conn.execute(INSERT INTO schema_migrations ...) except sqlite3.Error: raise (... chain aborted ...)
sites.why: Parallel SQLite migration runner of the same class: executescript() auto-commits the DDL, then the bookkeeping INSERT runs in a separate txn. If the INSERT fails after the DDL commits, the DB is 'ahead' of the ledger — relies on every migration's CREATE...IF NOT EXISTS being idempotent so the next apply_pending re-runs it. A failure here aborts the whole chain (same hard-stop semantics) and any non-idempotent future migration would double-apply.

The content-migration ledger is written to the IN-TREE repo content/ dir (_REPO = repo root), NOT user_data_root()/content where 0001/launcher actually copy data. Every other piece of the system (launcher.py:92, migrate_to_user_data.py:52, run_migrations.py:42) is user_data_root()-aware; this runner is not. Result: (a) frozen builds write the ledger into the read-only .app/.exe bundle -> save_state OSError or silent in-bundle write; (b) the version ledger and the copied user data live in two disconnected locations, so the ledger can never gate or repair the user-data copy. Core first-run/version-awareness gap of the runner class.
